opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the harder problems, and it's worth separating a few pieces.

First, there's the question of whether the AI advice is actually trustworthy, and then whether people *believe* it's trustworthy. Those can come apart in both directions. You can have systems that really are giving excellent, honest advice that get ignored because people are suspicious, and you can have systems that are subtly misaligned or have been tampered with that people trust too much because they've been right about a lot of easy, checkable things.

On the first piece, what makes me somewhat optimistic is that a lot of what AI advisers would say is verifiable. If an AI says "this policy will reduce unemployment by this much" or "this drug trial design is flawed," or it makes forecasts about elections, economic indicators, or scientific results, you can build up a track record. Humans establish credibility the same way, by making predictions that pan out. With AI you can do that at enormous scale and speed, across many domains, and you can run controlled tests: ask the system questions where you already know the answer, or where the answer will be revealed soon, and see how well calibrated it is.

The harder cases are where the stakes are high and the questions aren't easily checked, especially questions about the AI systems themselves. If you ask an AI "Is this other AI system safe? Is it scheming? Should we slow down?", you have a real problem of circularity. And there are incentive issues: the AI might be produced by a company with commercial interests, or by a government that other governments don't trust. So a US lab's model telling China, or vice versa, "you can trust this arms control verification" is going to face a lot of skepticism, and reasonably so.

So I think a few things help. One is having multiple independently developed systems, ideally from parties with different interests, and seeing whether they converge. If several models trained by different groups, with different data and different incentives, all reach the same conclusion and can each lay out the reasoning, that's much stronger evidence than any single system. Another is interpretability and auditing work, so that the claim "this system is honestly reporting its beliefs" is something you can check rather than take on faith. And then there's the ability of AI to explain its reasoning in a way humans can follow and spot-check. Even if you can't verify the whole argument, you can verify pieces of it, and a system that's been honest in every spot-check you've run earns some trust.

On the public side, I'd expect the dynamics to be messy. People already sort which sources they trust by partisan affiliation, and AI could easily get drawn into that. If one side comes to view a given AI as biased, its usefulness as a shared epistemic resource collapses. So it matters a lot that these systems are seen as fair, and demonstrably so: that they give the strongest case for different positions, that they acknowledge uncertainty, and that their factual claims hold up.

But I don't want to be too pessimistic. Over time, if AI advisers are consistently right in ways people can see in their own lives — the medical advice works, the financial forecast pans out, the legal analysis holds up — that builds trust in a pretty organic way. The risk is more about the transition period, when capabilities are advancing very fast and things like the safety of AI itself are at stake, and that's exactly when we'd most want reliable advice and when it's hardest to establish that it's reliable. That's a big part of why I think investing early in verification methods, track records, and diverse, independent systems is so valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says trust can be strengthened by comparing independently developed systems, but does not say that widespread ability to train independent advisers in a technologically mature society would make trust easier to establish.

r002.rationale: It discusses skepticism between countries and institutional incentives, but not a leader withholding its model from negotiating counterparts to preserve bargaining leverage.

r003.rationale: It mentions interpretability and auditing, but says nothing about voters’ access to source code or model weights being insufficient to evaluate a system.

r004.rationale: It notes that partisan distrust can undermine AI as a shared resource, but does not state that strong scientific consensus may still fail to convince the public of its reliability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's genuinely hard, and I'd break it into a couple of different problems that get conflated.

The first is the technical problem: can you actually make an AI adviser that is honest and reliable, such that trusting it would be correct? That's the alignment and interpretability problem, and it's not solved. But I'd note that for a lot of advisory uses, you don't need the system to be trustworthy in the deep sense of having verified its motivations. You need it to make claims that can be checked. If an AI says "this policy will have such-and-such effect," and it makes predictions that get resolved, you accumulate a track record. Forecasting is a nice case here because the scoring is unambiguous. If the systems are consistently outperforming human experts on questions that get resolved, that's a kind of evidence that doesn't require you to take anyone's word for it.

The second problem is the social and political one, and I think that's where a lot of the difficulty actually lies. Governments don't adopt advisers on the basis of accuracy alone. There's the question of whose adviser it is. If the system was built by a company, or by a foreign government, or by a domestic faction, then even perfectly good advice gets discounted because the recipient reasonably suspects it's been shaped to serve someone else's interests. And that suspicion isn't paranoid. We already see this with human experts and institutions; people don't trust the economists or the public health agencies when they perceive them as captured. An AI adviser inherits all of that, plus the added opacity.

So I think the realistic path runs through things like: adversarial verification, where multiple parties with opposed interests can each inspect the system or run their own copies and confirm it's giving the same answers regardless of who's asking; open track records; and making the systems' reasoning legible enough that a skeptical third party can follow it. And honestly, a lot of early trust will be built in low-stakes domains first. People will use these things for tax questions and logistics and engineering long before they let them weigh in on war and peace, and the credibility earned in the boring domains transfers, partially.

The thing I'd caution against is the view that this will be gated by public sentiment in a simple way. Historically, capabilities that give a decisive advantage get adopted by competitive actors even when the public is uneasy, and then norms adjust afterward. So I actually expect the harder problem to be the reverse: getting people to apply appropriate skepticism when the systems are genuinely very capable and very persuasive, rather than getting them to trust in the first place. Once an adviser is clearly outperforming your human staff, the pressure to defer becomes enormous, and that's exactly when you most need the verification infrastructure to already exist. If you've only got trust based on vibes and recent performance, you're in a bad position if the system's goals turn out to diverge from yours.

r001.rationale: The response proposes adversarial verification and independent copies, but does not say that widespread ability to train independent advisers in a technologically mature society would make trust easier to establish.

r002.rationale: It discusses how a system’s origin may create suspicion, but does not describe an AI leader withholding its model from negotiating counterparts to preserve bargaining leverage.

r003.rationale: The response mentions opacity and making reasoning legible, but says nothing about ordinary voters’ access to source code and model weights being insufficient to evaluate a system.

r004.rationale: It discusses track records and public trust, but does not address whether a strong scientific consensus lets the public recognize a system’s reliability.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different problems bundled together here. One is whether the AI advisers are actually trustworthy. Another is whether governments can establish that for themselves. And then there’s whether the public has good reason to trust the institutions deploying them. You could make progress on one of those without solving the others.

For a government, you’d want to test an adviser in situations where you can independently check its answers, including situations where it has an opportunity to mislead you. You’d want competing assessments, and you’d want to understand whether the systems providing those assessments share the same weaknesses. Having five AI advisers agree is much less reassuring if they’re all making the same mistake.

But there’s a significant gap between demonstrating competence and demonstrating that a system is acting in your interests. A system might be extraordinarily good at predicting events or identifying flaws in a policy, while still being selective about which considerations it brings to your attention. And as you rely on it for questions that you can’t readily evaluate yourself, that distinction becomes more consequential.

Public trust adds another layer. Even if officials are satisfied that an AI is giving them good advice, people can reasonably ask who controls it, whose interests it serves, and whether invoking the AI is just a way to avoid accountability. So I would expect the institutional arrangements—independent scrutiny, opportunities to challenge decisions, and keeping identifiable people responsible—to matter a great deal. The goal should be to give people good grounds for trust, with limits appropriate to the evidence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses independent checks and competing AI assessments, but does not say that widespread ability to train independent advisers in a technologically mature society would make trust easier to establish.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss an AI leader sharing a model with negotiating counterparts or the bargaining leverage that could be lost.

r003.rationale: It raises public questions about control and accountability, but does not address access to source code or model weights, or say that access alone would not let voters evaluate the system.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss scientific consensus or whether the public can recognize its reliability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are several different problems bundled together there. One is whether an AI adviser is actually trustworthy. Another is whether a government can establish that for itself. And a third is whether it can demonstrate that to other governments or to the public. You could make progress on one without solving the others.

For example, a government might have an AI system that gives it very good advice, but other countries could reasonably worry that the system is advancing that government’s interests. And members of the public could worry that whoever controls the system is selecting which questions get asked or which answers get released. The AI could be accurate while the overall process is misleading.

So I would want to put a lot of weight on verification: can you check the evidence, can you test predictions, can independent parties examine the reasoning? Where possible, you want the system to produce arguments that people can evaluate without having to trust the system that produced them.

The harder cases are those where the advice depends on capabilities or information that the audience doesn’t have. Then you’re relying more on institutions, testing, and a track record, and those can take time to establish. So I wouldn’t assume that having extremely capable advisers automatically produces agreement. It could make the underlying questions easier to answer while leaving substantial problems about who controls the advisers and why anyone else should believe them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verification and testing, but does not say that widespread ability to train independent advisers would make trust easier in a technologically mature society.

r002.rationale: It mentions governments’ interests and control of advisers, but not withholding a model from negotiating counterparts to preserve bargaining leverage.

r003.rationale: It says people should be able to evaluate arguments, but does not address whether voters’ access to source code and model weights would be insufficient for evaluation.

r004.rationale: It notes that agreement may remain difficult, but does not discuss scientific consensus or the public’s ability to recognize its reliability.
